sections.h2: Is there a quitclaim deed in Louisiana?
sections.html:
Not by that name. Louisiana law has no form called a quitclaim deed. The nearest equivalent is Civil Code article 2502, which lets a person transfer whatever rights he has in a thing without warranting that those rights exist.

Under that article the transferor owes no refund of the price if the transferee is later evicted, and the transfer cannot be rescinded for lesion. Louisiana is a civil law state, so deed vocabulary comes from the Civil Code. The Orleans Parish clerk describes a deed as an Act of Sale, which may take the form of a Cash Sale, Credit Sale or Warranty Deed.

So expect the paper you sign to carry a Civil Code title such as act of sale, not the words quitclaim deed.

sections.h2: What a transfer without warranty does and does not do
sections.html:
The buyer receives the seller's rights as they stand and carries the risk that they are weaker than hoped. Article 2502 adds a few more points for anyone choosing this route.

  • The transfer raises no presumption that the buyer acted in bad faith.
  • It counts as a just title for acquisitive prescription, so a buyer who then holds the land can build toward ten years of possession.
  • If the seller later acquires ownership of the thing, that later title does not pass to the buyer.
  • The seller does not guarantee a refund of the price if a third party wins the property.

A full sale works differently. Under article 2503 the warranty against eviction is implied in every sale, and the parties may enlarge or limit it. Even when they exclude it, the seller must return the price after an eviction unless the buyer clearly knew of the risk, declared the purchase to be at his own risk, or the refund duty was expressly excluded. A seller is always liable for an eviction caused by his own act, and a contrary agreement is void.

Article 2500 defines eviction as the buyer's loss, or danger of losing, all or part of the thing sold because of a third party's earlier right, including undisclosed encumbrances.

A transfer of immovable property must be made by authentic act or by act under private signature, under article 1839. An oral transfer can bind the parties only in narrow cases, where the property was delivered and the transferor admits the transfer under oath.

An authentic act under article 1833 is a writing executed before a notary public or other authorized officer and two witnesses. The parties, witnesses and notary all sign, and a party who cannot sign makes a mark at the notary's direction. Closings usually run through a notary for that reason.

  • Effect against third persons begins only when the deed is filed in the parish (C.C. art. 1839).
  • The deed must name the person responsible for taxes and a notice address (La. R.S. 9:2721).

sections.h2: Where a Louisiana deed is recorded
sections.html:
File the deed with the clerk of court, acting as recorder, in the parish where the property sits. Until it is filed there, the instrument does not bind third persons.

Orleans Parish shows how the process runs. Its Land Records Division at 1340 Poydras Street accepts documents by mail, in person or through eRecording vendors, and a cover sheet tells the office to record in the mortgage records, the conveyance records, or both. Clerk staff cannot tell you which documents to file.

Any deed filed in Louisiana must name the person responsible for taxes and give a mailing address for tax notices. That person passes the details to the assessor so bills reach the right place.

Parish clerks set their own hours, payment methods and add-on charges, so call before mailing a check.

La. R.S. 13:844 sets the base fee at $100 for one to five pages, $200 for six to 25 pages and $300 for 26 to 50 pages, plus $5 for each page above 50.

ServiceFee
Recording, 1 to 5 pages$100

The base fee covers indexing up to ten names and one certified copy. A document recorded in both the mortgage and conveyance records is charged separately for each, and paper other than 8.5 by 11 or 8.5 by 14 inches adds $20 a page.

Orleans Parish adds a $5 remote access portal fee and a $30 courthouse building fund fee per recording. The city also charges a $325 documentary transaction tax on sales. Other parishes have their own add-ons.

The Orleans clerk's Land Records Division will reject or surcharge documents with bad margins, and it does not take personal checks.

  • The first page needs a two inch top margin, and every page needs one inch at the bottom and both sides, or a $20 surcharge applies.
  • The first page must carry a caption naming the type of act, in type no smaller than eight point.
  • By mail, send a business check or money order payable to Clerk of Court.
  • eRecording is available through CSC, ePN and Simplifile.
  • A cover sheet marks the document for the mortgage records, the conveyance records or both.

A recorded sale there also triggers the documentary transaction tax of $325 per taxable document, which falls on the seller. It is paid at recording or billed, and a bill unpaid after 30 days adds interest and a $500 penalty.

sections.h2: When a transfer of rights works for a seller
sections.html:
It can suit a transfer between family members, a cleanup of a boundary or interest, or a case where the seller honestly cannot vouch for title. It fits poorly when the buyer pays full price and needs title insurance.

  • Heirs who have not finished a succession may hold only uncertain rights.
  • A divorce settlement can move one spouse's interest to the other.
  • A buyer who needs the seller to stand behind the title should ask for a full sale with the implied warranty left in place.

Moving title does not erase a mortgage, tax lien or judgment. A recorded mortgage stays on the record until a cancellation is filed, and Orleans Parish charges $50 to record the cancellation of a single mortgage.

If you want to sell a house with unclear title, an inherited share or a lien, we can read the record with you and explain what a closing would need.

faqs.q: Is a quitclaim deed valid in Louisiana?
faqs.a: Louisiana has no deed by that name, but article 2502 of the Civil Code lets you transfer the rights you hold without warranting them. The recorded paper is usually an act of sale, donation or transfer of rights, and it must meet the form rules for immovable property.

faqs.q: Does a Louisiana deed need a notary?
faqs.a: A transfer of immovable property can be an authentic act or an act under private signature. An authentic act is signed before a notary or other authorized officer and two witnesses, which is why most closings use a notary.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Louisiana?
faqs.a: File it with the clerk of court in the parish where the property is located. The instrument affects third persons only from the time it is filed there. In Orleans Parish that is the Land Records Division at 1340 Poydras Street.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Louisiana?
faqs.a: The base fee is $100 for one to five pages, $200 for six to 25 pages and $300 for 26 to 50 pages. Orleans Parish adds a $5 portal fee and a $30 building fund fee, and other parishes may add their own charges.

faqs.q: Does the seller still warrant title with a no warranty transfer?
faqs.a: Not for the rights themselves, since under article 2502 no refund is owed if the buyer is evicted. The seller stays liable for his own acts, because article 2503 voids any agreement excusing an eviction he caused.
